issues.subcategory: inconsistent study aim/hypothesis direction
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between asking whether moral incongruence generalizes across addictions and stating a specific goal of demonstrating that it is unique to pornography/sexual behavior. This creates ambiguity about whether the registered report is confirmatory, exploratory, or advocacy-driven, and may bias interpretation of null/non-null findings across domains.
issues.quote: "The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence ... is uniquely related to sexual behavior, or if it generalizes to other addictions as well." ... "with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors."

issues.subcategory: inconsistent definition of moral incongruence
issues.description: Moral incongruence is repeatedly defined as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but later is described as the interaction between moral disapproval and severity of consequences. This is a substantive conceptual and analytic inconsistency because severity/consequences are part of the outcome/problem construct, not merely exposure frequency; using consequences in the interaction would risk circularity and change the hypothesis being tested.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior)" ... "Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action."

issues.subcategory: non-representative combined sample
issues.description: The study describes a representative U.S. sample plus a large sports-wagering oversample, then often refers to the total N=4,000 as a representative or population sample. Combining a representative sample with an enriched sports-betting sample without clearly specifying weighting, stratification, or separate analyses compromises prevalence estimates, associations involving gambling, and generalizability to the U.S. population.
issues.quote: "representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500)" ... "This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults."

issues.subcategory: missing weighting and matching details
issues.description: YouGov matching is mentioned, but the manuscript does not specify the sampling frame, response/recruitment procedures, post-stratification variables, use of survey weights, whether analyses will be weighted, or how the oversample will be handled. These details are necessary to evaluate representativeness, design effects, standard errors, and population inference.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms."

issues.subcategory: overclaim from population sample with oversample
issues.description: The authors claim the study can evaluate effects at a population level, but the analytic plan does not establish nationally representative weighting or correction for the sports-betting oversample. Population-level claims may therefore be unsupported.
issues.quote: "despite the ability of the present study to evaluate whether or not moral incongruence affects self-reported feelings of addiction a population level"

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval for all behaviors is measured with one face-valid item. Single items cannot estimate reliability, may not capture the multidimensional nature of moral judgment, stigma, legality, health concerns, religious prohibition, or self-directed distress, and may behave differently across substances and behaviors. This threatens comparability across domains and the validity of the central moderator.
issues.quote: "we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions" ... "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval not equivalent to moral incongruence or distress
issues.description: The theoretical construct includes moral incongruence and moral distress, but the operationalization measures only general moral wrongness of the behavior. It does not assess whether participants perceive their own use as violating personal values, whether they experience distress, guilt, shame, or whether the disapproval applies to others versus self. This creates a construct mismatch with claims about moral distress in CSBD and false positive diagnosis.
issues.quote: "distress related to moral disapproval of one’s own sexual behaviors" ... "I believe that pornography use is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: nonvalidated modification of ASSIST
issues.description: The ASSIST/NIDA Quick Screen is substantially modified: behaviors such as pornography and gambling are added, response categories are changed, and items are averaged across heterogeneous response scales. These modifications may invalidate scoring, psychometric properties, and clinical interpretation, particularly for comparisons across substances and behaviors.
issues.quote: "We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST" ... "Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography"

issues.subcategory: averaging incompatible ASSIST item metrics
issues.description: The proposed problematic-use score averages three 0–5 frequency items with two items scored 0, 3, and 6. These items have different time frames, distributions, and scale ranges; a simple average gives disproportionate influence to lifetime/current concern and control items and has no validated meaning as an ASSIST score.
issues.quote: "Participants will respond to three frequency based questions ... on a scale of 0 ... to 5 ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged"

issues.subcategory: mixed time frames between predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavioral frequency is assessed over the past 12 months, pornography problems over the past 6 months, several ASSIST symptoms over the past 3 months, and some control/concern items over lifetime or past 3 months. These mismatched windows impair interpretation of frequency–problem associations and interactions, and may attenuate or inflate domain-specific effects.
issues.quote: "past-year frequency" ... "In the last 6 months" ... "In the past three months" ... "Have you ever tried and failed"

issues.subcategory: dependent variables include moral/guilt content
issues.description: The BPS and PGSI outcomes include items about guilt or feeling guilty, which overlap conceptually with moral disapproval/moral incongruence. This can inflate associations between morality and self-reported addiction/problem scores via item contamination rather than genuine dysregulation.
issues.quote: "You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it." ... "Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?"

issues.subcategory: outcome conflates self-perceived addiction with validated symptom severity
issues.description: The manuscript frequently describes outcomes as self-reported feelings of addiction, but planned outcomes include the BPS, PGSI, and modified ASSIST symptom/problem scores. These instruments assess overlapping but different constructs: perceived addiction, screening risk, consequences, urges, impairment, and problem severity. Treating them as equivalent can obscure interpretation.
issues.quote: "self-reported feelings of addiction" ... "problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index" ... "problematic or potentially addictive use ... average of responses to problematic use questions"

issues.subcategory: selection on behavior engagement conditions on collider/use status
issues.description: The plan appears to analyze only participants reporting past-year use for each behavior, while moral disapproval and problematic-use measures are administered to all participants. Restricting to users can be appropriate for some questions, but it changes the estimand, may induce selection bias if moral disapproval affects abstention, and excludes highly disapproving non-users who are theoretically informative for moral incongruence.
issues.quote: "only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months ... will complete the remaining items" ... "for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample"

issues.subcategory: contradictory administration plan
issues.description: The manuscript first says only users will complete further/problematic-use measures, but later says key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This affects sample sizes, missingness, zero-inflation, scoring, and the analytic population for each model.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use." ... "key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample."

issues.subcategory: frequency scale coding inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes modified frequency scales as 0–5 and 1–6. This matters for centering, interpretation of intercepts, inclusion criteria, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: "on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)" ... "on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)"

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods state that BPS items are scored 0 to 2, whereas the supplemental table uses 0, 2, and 4. This leads to different total-score ranges and affects clinical/screening interpretation and regression scaling.
issues.quote: "on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed." ... "Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)"

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods describe the PGSI as a 0–3 scale, but the supplemental materials score responses as 0, 2, 4, and 5. The standard PGSI is typically 0–3 and summed. This discrepancy compromises replicability and the validity of severity classification or continuous scoring.
issues.quote: "on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged." ... "Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)"

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measure contradiction
issues.description: The text says gambling frequency will be assessed with a single item, but also says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials show only one item. This creates ambiguity about what predictor will be used.
issues.quote: "We will assess gambling frequency using a single item." ... "To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken."

issues.subcategory: number of moderation analyses inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript refers to eight proposed outcomes and eight moderation analyses, but lists seven target behavior categories in the analytic paragraph, and Table 1 implies nine outcomes if pornography and gambling each have validated and modified ASSIST outcomes. This ambiguity affects multiplicity correction, preregistration specificity, and interpretation of confirmatory tests.
issues.quote: "for each of the eight proposed outcomes" ... "8 target behaviors/variables of interest" ... "pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures ..."

issues.subcategory: incorrect or unclear equivalence-test parameter
issues.description: The analytic plan states an equivalence region with SESOI δ=.27, but then explains that the chosen SESOI is β=.11 and that δ=|.11| is conservative. These inconsistent equivalence bounds would lead to different conclusions about whether effects are practically null.
issues.quote: "with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27." ... "setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision"

issues.subcategory: mixing standardized beta, f2, d, and delta without clear transformation
issues.description: The plan uses δ for equivalence, standardized beta values, ΔR2, f2, and Cohen's d interchangeably. It is unclear which metric reg.equiv.fd will use and how equivalence bounds are transformed for each model. Misalignment of metrics can make equivalence tests invalid or uninterpretable.

issues.subcategory: incorrect direct conversion of interaction effect sizes
issues.description: The manuscript presents Cohen's d values corresponding to ΔR2/f2 for regression interactions without explaining the conversion and appears to equate interaction ΔR2 with standardized beta. For regression interactions, these conversions depend on model structure and predictor distributions; unsupported conversions can misstate prior effect sizes and SESOI justification.
issues.quote: "small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen’s d = .24 ... ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22), to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen’s d = .69)"

issues.subcategory: power analysis ignores survey design and oversampling
issues.description: Power analyses assume simple random sampling and independent observations with fixed N. They do not account for survey weights, matching, design effects, or the nonrepresentative sports-betting oversample, which can reduce effective sample size and alter precision, especially for gambling analyses.
issues.quote: "All analyses conducted using G*power; assuming α = 0.05, regression models with 6 independent variables"

issues.subcategory: power based on prevalence estimates may be inaccurate in oversampled design
issues.description: Effective Ns are calculated by applying general-population prevalence estimates to the total sample of 4,000, despite the additional 1,500 sports-wagering adults who likely differ in substance use, gambling, gender, age, and other correlates. Effective Ns and power may therefore be inaccurate.
issues.quote: "Estimated percentage of sample engaging in behavior" ... "Effective N"

issues.subcategory: underpowered rare-substance analyses
issues.description: The authors acknowledge low power for prescription drug misuse and illicit substances but still frame tests as hypothesis-relevant. The proposed fallback equivalence region changes the research question rather than solving low power for the original SESOI, and null/equivalence conclusions for these subgroups may be unreliable.
issues.quote: "Prescription Drug Misuse ... Effective N 140 ... Estimated Achieved power for f2= .015 .301" ... "Illicit Substances ... .472-.764"

issues.subcategory: post hoc equivalence-bound adjustment
issues.description: The plan allows changing the equivalence region after seeing whether effects exceed the primary SESOI and based on the observed pornography effect. This creates researcher degrees of freedom and can make conclusions about uniqueness dependent on data-contingent thresholds.
issues.quote: "In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects ... exceed our region of equivalence ... we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome."

issues.subcategory: vague supplemental analyses for assumption violations
issues.description: The manuscript states that supplemental analyses will be conducted if regression assumptions are substantially violated, but does not define substantial violation or specify alternative models. This leaves substantial analytic flexibility, especially because outcomes are ordinal, zero-inflated, and bounded.
issues.quote: "in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate"

issues.subcategory: OLS for bounded ordinal/skewed outcomes
issues.description: The planned OLS regressions may be inappropriate for outcomes that are summed/averaged ordinal items with strong skew, floor effects, and zero-inflation among community samples. Without specifying count/ordinal/zero-inflated or robust alternatives, estimates, standard errors, and interaction tests may be biased or inefficient.
issues.quote: "we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R"

issues.subcategory: treating ordinal frequency predictors as interval linear variables
issues.description: Behavior frequency is measured using coarse ordinal categories from never to more than once per day, but the plan treats frequency as a centered continuous predictor. The distances between categories are not equal, and a linear interaction may misrepresent dose-response relationships.
issues.quote: "participants will report ... frequency ... Never to Daily or Almost Daily ... adding ... more than once per day" ... "focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators ... will be centered and their interaction term calculated"

issues.subcategory: multiple comparisons not adequately controlled for primary hypotheses
issues.description: The study plans numerous regressions across substances/behaviors and multiple outcomes but does not specify correction or hierarchical testing for the primary moderation/equivalence tests. Holm adjustment is mentioned only for bivariate correlations. This increases false-positive risk and ambiguity about confirmatory inference.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses" ... "Bivariate correlations will be conducted ... using Holm-adjusted test statistics"

issues.subcategory: Holm-adjusted test statistics terminology
issues.description: Holm adjustment applies to p-values, not test statistics. The phrase suggests imprecision in the planned reporting of correlations and multiplicity adjustment.
issues.quote: "reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics"

issues.subcategory: insufficient model specification
issues.description: The analytic plan does not fully specify model formulas, whether predictors/outcomes will be standardized before equivalence tests, whether covariates are entered simultaneously, handling of nonbinary gender categories, weighting, robust SEs, or whether validated and modified outcomes are primary versus secondary. This limits reproducibility of the registered report.
issues.quote: "moderation analyses using the lm function" ... "key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed"

issues.subcategory: raw versus centered variables contradiction
issues.description: The plan states predictors and moderators will be centered and interaction terms calculated, but later says key variables will be entered in raw form and their product computed. Centering affects interpretation and can affect numerical stability and equivalence-test scaling if standardization is involved.
issues.quote: "focal predictors ... and moderators ... will be centered and their interaction term calculated" ... "key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed"

issues.subcategory: covariate set insufficient for confounding
issues.description: Only age, gender, and religiousness are planned covariates. Potential confounders such as socioeconomic status, education, race/ethnicity, political ideology, mental health, impulsivity, availability/legal status, relationship status, and overall substance/behavior involvement may influence both moral disapproval and perceived problems. This limits causal or uniqueness interpretations of associations.
issues.quote: "we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates"

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional correlational data
issues.description: The study is cross-sectional, yet the manuscript uses causal language such as moral incongruence influencing, affecting, or contributing to feelings of addiction. Cross-sectional moderation cannot establish temporal order or causal effects; perceived problems may increase moral disapproval, and third variables may explain associations.
issues.quote: "whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction" ... "moral incongruence affects self-reported feelings of addiction"

issues.subcategory: reverse causation unaddressed
issues.description: People experiencing problematic use may become more morally disapproving of the behavior after negative consequences, treatment exposure, social conflict, or attempts to quit. The design cannot distinguish moral disapproval causing perceived addiction from addiction/problems causing moral disapproval.
issues.quote: "moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems"

issues.subcategory: uniqueness inference from null interactions
issues.description: The authors propose that finding interactions only for pornography would support the uniqueness of CSBD moral caveats. But absence or equivalence of statistical interactions in self-report survey data for selected substances does not demonstrate that moral distress is uniquely clinically relevant to CSBD, nor that diagnostic caveats are valid only there. Domain differences in measurement, prevalence, stigma, legality, and outcome contamination complicate this inference.
issues.quote: "Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress."

issues.subcategory: overextension from pornography to CSBD
issues.description: The empirical study focuses primarily on pornography use, yet discussion frames implications for CSBD, which includes broader sexual behaviors and requires clinical impairment/dysregulation. Pornography self-report scores in a community survey are not equivalent to CSBD diagnosis.
issues.quote: "should we find that moral incongruence ... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence ... supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD"

issues.subcategory: pornography use limited to solitary viewing
issues.description: The supplemental pornography frequency item assesses only viewing pornography alone, while moral disapproval and BPS items refer to pornography use generally. This mismatch may misclassify partnered pornography use and reduce construct validity of the frequency predictor.
issues.quote: "Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)"

issues.subcategory: alcohol frequency not quantity-specific
issues.description: The authors choose general alcohol frequency rather than binge/heavy drinking frequency for the primary predictor. General use frequency may poorly represent exposure relevant to alcohol use disorder symptoms and is not parallel to prescription drug misuse or illegal drug use in terms of inherent problem status.
issues.quote: "we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed)"

issues.subcategory: gender-specific drinking item labeling error
issues.description: For men, the manuscript says more than 5 drinks but the table labels the row as 'More than four drinks'. This threatens accurate implementation of the NIDA Quick Screen and reproducibility.
issues.quote: "IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)"

issues.subcategory: prescription drug moral item confounds behavior with misuse
issues.description: Prescription drug frequency is for non-medical reasons and moral disapproval is of using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons, whereas the target behavior in Table 1 is labeled 'Prescription Drug Use/Misuse'. The construct is misuse rather than general prescription use, making comparisons to legal/common behaviors like alcohol and pornography asymmetric.
issues.quote: "Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons" ... "I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: illicit drug moral disapproval confounded with legality
issues.description: For illegal/illicit drugs, moral disapproval may reflect legal status, perceived danger, social desirability, or stigma rather than personal moral incongruence. This undermines comparability with pornography, alcohol, and gambling, where legality varies differently.
issues.quote: "I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong."

issues.subcategory: no blinding or demand-characteristic mitigation
issues.description: Participants answer moral disapproval items and problem/addiction items in the same survey, likely close together and with highly similar wording. Without randomized order, separation, or demand-characteristic controls, responses may be inflated by consistency motifs or shared method variance.
issues.quote: "we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample"

issues.subcategory: missing item order and survey flow details
issues.description: The manuscript provides measures but not the exact order, branching, randomization, attention checks, or whether moral disapproval is assessed before or after problem items. Order effects could be substantial when moral judgments and perceived problems are assessed together.
issues.quote: "Key measures described below are available in supplemental materials"

issues.subcategory: unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The manuscript assumes no unplanned missingness because YouGov collects the data. Online panel data can still contain item nonresponse, breakoffs, routing errors, 'prefer not to answer' responses, or missing panel covariates. No missing data handling plan is provided.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data."

issues.subcategory: no handling plan for panel covariate missingness
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are drawn from panel data, not the study survey. The plan does not specify how outdated, missing, nonbinary, or inconsistent panel covariate data will be handled.
issues.quote: "Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey)."

issues.subcategory: quality-control reliance on proprietary standards
issues.description: The authors state no exclusions are expected because YouGov guarantees quality control via proprietary standards. Without specifying attention checks, speed thresholds, duplicate handling, fraud detection, or exclusion criteria, data quality cannot be independently evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: "certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed ... based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses"

issues.subcategory: registered report preregistration details incomplete
issues.description: Although described as a registered report/pre-registered design, the manuscript does not provide registry location, hypotheses numbering consistency, analysis scripts, data/code availability plan, or clear distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses beyond some post hoc plans.
issues.quote: "A Registered Report" ... "pre-registered design"

issues.subcategory: binary gender coding excludes nonbinary participants
issues.description: The visualization/moderation plan codes gender as 1=male and 0=not-male. This collapses women and gender-diverse participants, may mishandle nonbinary or missing gender, and is inconsistent with sex-specific alcohol screening branches that only mention woman/man.
issues.quote: "gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)"

issues.subcategory: no plan for multicollinearity in interaction models
issues.description: Moral disapproval and religiousness are likely highly correlated, and interaction terms can increase collinearity. The plan does not specify diagnostics or remedies. Multicollinearity may inflate standard errors and complicate equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: "religiousness, age, and gender as covariates" ... "moral disapproval ... frequency ... interaction"

issues.subcategory: equivalence testing for standardized effects not fully specified
issues.description: Equivalence tests are said to be based on standardized effects, but the plan also says raw variables will be used. Standardized interaction coefficients are scale-dependent and can vary with subgroup restriction and outcome distributions. Without explicit standardization procedures, equivalence bounds cannot be replicated.
issues.quote: "Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction ... fall fully within our equivalence region" ... "key variables will be entered in their raw form"

issues.subcategory: assumption of independent residuals insufficiently justified
issues.description: Participants are recruited from an online panel and include oversampled sports bettors. There may be clustering by recruitment source, panel strata, state/legal gambling environment, or household. The plan merely tests independence of residuals but gives no design-based model or clustered SE plan.
issues.quote: "assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity, independence of residuals...) will be tested"

issues.subcategory: legal context not measured or modeled
issues.description: Cannabis and gambling legality vary substantially by U.S. state and may affect both moral disapproval and frequency/problems. State is available in panel data, but the plan does not use legal status or regional context, leaving an important confound and moderator unaddressed.
issues.quote: "given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S." ... "State of Residence"

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only cultural limitation understated relative to claims
issues.description: The authors note the U.S. context limitation, but much of the theoretical and diagnostic discussion concerns ICD-11 and addiction nosology broadly. U.S. moral, religious, legal, and gambling contexts may not generalize internationally.
issues.quote: "such a sample represents only one broad cultural context" ... "would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD"

issues.subcategory: cross-sectional self-report only
issues.description: All key constructs are self-reported in one survey, increasing common method variance, social desirability bias, recall bias, and shared negative affect. No clinical interviews, behavioral records, collateral reports, or temporal design are included to distinguish perceived addiction from dysregulation.
issues.quote: "self-reported feelings of addiction" ... "Participants will be asked how often"

issues.subcategory: religiousness composite may be psychometrically problematic
issues.description: The religiousness composite averages standardized ordinal items with different response scales and content. The plan does not specify treatment of denominational differences, nonreligious participants, or measurement invariance. Standardizing before averaging makes interpretation sample-dependent.
issues.quote: "Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items"

issues.subcategory: tobacco/non-tobacco nicotine category inconsistency
issues.description: The methods say outcomes include tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis, but later tables collapse tobacco/nicotine products into one category. This affects the claimed number of substances and analyses.
issues.quote: "for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis)" ... "Tobacco/Nicotine products"

issues.subcategory: validated measures typo reflects ambiguity
issues.description: The analytic plan says pornography and gambling will be assessed using 'the validate measures', and Table 1 also lists modified ASSIST items. It is unclear whether validated measures are primary and ASSIST outcomes secondary, or both are confirmatory.
issues.quote: "with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use"

issues.subcategory: no clinical diagnostic validation
issues.description: The manuscript makes claims about recognized addictive disorders and diagnostic caveats, but does not assess DSM/ICD diagnoses or clinical impairment through structured interviews. Screening and self-report problem scales cannot establish disorder status.
issues.quote: "recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders" ... "self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms"

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency too broad and heterogeneous
issues.description: A single frequency item collapses lottery tickets, casino gambling, fantasy sports, online betting, cards, esports, and sports betting. These differ in risk, frequency norms, legality, and moral meaning. Averaging or using one item may obscure meaningful exposure and weaken construct validity.
issues.quote: "Examples ... gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money, placing bets on esports, placing bets on traditional sporting events, playing cards for money, placing bets online."

issues.subcategory: possible sparse data and floor effects for disapproved/rare behaviors
issues.description: Prescription drug misuse and illicit drug use will have small user subsamples, likely skewed moral disapproval and problem scores, and limited variation. Linear interaction estimates and equivalence tests may be unstable.
issues.quote: "prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population)"

issues.subcategory: ambiguous primary outcome for pornography and gambling
issues.description: For pornography and gambling, both validated scales and modified ASSIST items are planned. The manuscript does not clearly designate which outcome tests the primary hypotheses, creating multiple ways to support or disconfirm uniqueness.
issues.quote: "Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items" ... "Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items"

issues.subcategory: misleading claim CSBD caveat implies unique role of morality
issues.description: The manuscript infers that because CSBD uniquely includes a moral-distress caveat, morality may have a unique role in CSBD. Diagnostic manuals may include caveats for historical, political, or differential-diagnosis reasons; absence of caveats elsewhere does not imply morality is absent or less important in other disorders.
issues.quote: "At present, CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat, pointing to the unique role of morality"

issues.subcategory: hypothesis asymmetry favors desired conclusion
issues.description: The authors hypothesize direct moral-disapproval effects for gambling/substances but null interactions, while expecting both direct and interaction effects for pornography. However, the theoretical rationale for why moral disapproval would affect problem reports but not interact with frequency outside pornography is underdeveloped and may reflect confirmatory bias rather than a strong competing theory.
issues.quote: "we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems" ... "we do not expect to find that the interactions ... will contribute uniquely"

issues.subcategory: missing recruitment timing/context relative to gambling season
issues.description: Data collection is planned for late March 2022, during NCAA March Madness and after expansion of sports betting in many states. The manuscript does not discuss how seasonal betting context may affect sports wagering, gambling frequency, or problem reports.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors"

issues.subcategory: table formatting/content corruption
issues.description: Table 2 and supplemental tables contain duplicated footnote text across columns and repeated headers, making the sample-size and power information difficult to verify. This undermines clarity and replicability.
issues.quote: "1. All substance estimates based on ... | 1. All substance estimates based on ... | 1. All substance estimates based on ..."

issues.subcategory: PGSI averaged rather than standard summed/categorized scoring
issues.description: The methods say PGSI responses will be averaged, while standard PGSI scoring typically sums items and uses established cutoffs. Averaging is mathematically proportional only if scoring is correct, but it changes interpretability and may not align with validation evidence or clinical categories.
issues.quote: "Responses will be averaged."

issues.subcategory: BPS summed but modified response scoring alters validation
issues.description: The BPS is described as validated, but the supplemental response scoring appears to double the usual 0–2 item scores to 0–4. If implemented, cutoffs and psychometric properties from validation studies no longer directly apply.
issues.quote: "This five-item measure has been validated" ... "Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)"

issues.subcategory: no plan for scale reliability with single-item measures
issues.description: The analytic plan says internal consistency will be calculated for included scales, but central moral disapproval measures and frequency predictors are single items. The manuscript does not discuss reliability limitations or measurement error attenuation for interaction terms.
issues.quote: "measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total)"

issues.subcategory: interaction measurement error not addressed
issues.description: Interactions involving single-item moral disapproval and coarse ordinal frequency will be measured with substantial error, reducing power and biasing effects toward zero. This is especially problematic because the study's central inference depends on finding null/equivalent interactions outside pornography.
issues.quote: "single-item moral disapproval questions" ... "frequency ... 6-point scale"

issues.subcategory: potential confounding by negative affect/stigma
issues.description: Self-reported problem severity and moral disapproval may both reflect general shame, stigma sensitivity, depression, anxiety, or negative affectivity. Without measuring or adjusting for these, the observed moral incongruence effects may not reflect moral conflict per se.
issues.quote: "both negatively valenced judgments about the same behavior"

issues.subcategory: no control for behavior-specific norms and harms
issues.description: Substances differ markedly in physiological dependence, legal consequences, social harms, and normative frequency. A common interaction model across behaviors may not isolate morality because frequency and problems have different meanings across alcohol, nicotine, illicit drugs, gambling, and pornography.
issues.quote: "These will be included to allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors and substances (i.e., everything will be on the exact same scale using the exact same measurements)."

issues.subcategory: frequency scale ceiling inadequate for nicotine and possibly pornography
issues.description: Adding 'more than once per day' may still be too crude for nicotine use, where multiple uses per day are normative and dependence severity depends on intensity, latency, and quantity. This can compress variance and reduce validity of the frequency predictor.
issues.quote: "given that we are including behaviors that likely occur multiple times per day for many users (i.e., nicotine use) we will modify response options by adding an additional frequency category of more than once per day"

issues.subcategory: substance categories omit dosage/intensity
issues.description: For alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, and illicit substances, use frequency alone omits quantity, potency, route of administration, and binge patterns, all of which are central to addiction risk and problem severity. This weakens tests of frequency by morality interactions.
issues.quote: "we will look at alcohol frequency more generally" ... "how often they have used the following"

issues.subcategory: no data exclusion/inclusion threshold for incomplete scales
issues.description: The plan does not specify how scale scores will be computed if some items are missing, whether prorating will be used, or minimum item completion thresholds. This is necessary even if missingness is expected to be low.
issues.quote: "Scale scores for included measures will also be calculated in SPSS."

issues.subcategory: ambiguous robustness criterion
issues.description: The plan says OLS will be retained if sign and significance remain the same across analytic techniques, but does not define which result is authoritative if magnitude, equivalence, or confidence intervals differ. Equivalence conclusions depend on CI bounds, not only sign/significance.
issues.quote: "Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results"

issues.subcategory: significance logic conflicts with equivalence logic
issues.description: The robustness criterion focuses on sign and significance, but the hypotheses for gambling/substances depend on equivalence testing rather than nonsignificance. A result can be nonsignificant but not equivalent, or significant but practically equivalent depending on N and SESOI. The plan does not fully integrate these inferential frameworks.
issues.quote: "sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same" ... "equivalence tests will reveal the effect ... to fall within the equivalence interval"

issues.subcategory: sports-wagering funding/context potential conflict not methodologically addressed
issues.description: The larger study is funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming and oversamples sports wagerers. Although not necessarily invalidating, the manuscript does not describe conflict-of-interest safeguards, independence of analysis, or whether survey content/order is shaped by the larger project, which may affect gambling-related measures.
issues.quote: "funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming"

issues.subcategory: sample size described as over 4000 but exactly 4000 target
issues.description: The manuscript states N=4,000 and also 'over 4,000' despite target components totaling exactly 4,000. This is minor but reflects imprecision in planned sample size reporting.
issues.quote: "N=4,000" ... "This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults."

issues.subcategory: model count excludes race/education despite matched sample
issues.description: The sample is matched to age and gender only, but other demographic imbalances may remain. The analysis does not include race, education, income, or region despite their availability and likely associations with morality and substance/gambling behaviors. This may bias associations and reduce external validity.
issues.quote: "match nationally representative norms for age and gender" ... "YouGov Panel Data Included ... Race Education ... Family income ... State"

issues.subcategory: ASSIST item wording awkward for behaviors
issues.description: ASSIST items originally designed for substances are adapted to 'use of or engagement in' pornography/gambling. Some items such as strong urge, failed obligations, health/legal/financial problems may have different salience and severity across behaviors, weakening claims of parallel measurement.
issues.quote: "how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?"

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence interaction may not capture discrepancy
issues.description: An interaction between frequency and disapproval does not directly measure discrepancy or incongruence. A person with high disapproval and low use, or moderate disapproval and high use, may experience moral conflict differently. More direct measures or polynomial/profile approaches may be needed to model value-behavior misalignment.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use"

issues.subcategory: simple slopes/probing not specified
issues.description: The plan says interactions will be visualized but does not specify simple slopes, Johnson-Neyman regions, or how the predicted pattern will be evaluated. A positive interaction alone may not establish the hypothesized stronger frequency-problem relationship among disapprovers if main effects/scaling differ.
issues.quote: "To visualize results ... Interactive Shiny application"

issues.subcategory: no plan for handling zero-frequency participants in outcome measures
issues.description: If non-users complete problem measures, their scores should logically be zero or not applicable. The plan does not specify whether non-users are included with zero outcome scores, excluded, or treated as missing. This choice materially changes regression estimates.
issues.quote: "we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample"
